query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy, the coexistence of chemically and electrochemically dissimilar phases creates localized micro‐galvanic cells that, when combined with mechanical wear at elevated temperatures, lead to the accelerated removal of protective oxide layers and preferential corrosion of the more anodic phase. This feedback between wear-induced exposure and galvanic corrosion at the phase boundaries enhances both the wear and corrosion rates synergistically.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic HEA with a lamellar (or interpenetrating) microstructure comprising at least two phases that differ in corrosion resistance and electrochemical potential (e.g., a relatively noble phase and a more anodic phase).
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., reciprocating sliding under controlled load) and a corrosive environment at an elevated temperature.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., in the range of 450–650 °C), in a corrosive medium (such as an acidic solution or salt environment) with a prescribed mechanical load and wear cycling that together simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The heterogeneity at interphase boundaries promotes micro‐galvanic coupling; the differential electrochemical potentials between the phases cause selective oxidation/corrosion, particularly when wear strips off the nascent protective oxide layers.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear repeatedly removes or disrupts protective oxide films that naturally form on the more noble phase. This exposes fresh surfaces and increases the local contact between phases with differing electrochemical behaviors. The resulting micro‐galvanic cells accelerate the corrosion of the more anodic phase while the mechanical damage further weakens the interface, leading to a synergistic increase in both wear damage and corrosion degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a homogenized single‐phase alloy baseline, the multi‐phase eutectic HEA will exhibit a higher overall degradation rate. Specifically, the wear component will be intensified due to deeper pit formation and material removal at the phase boundaries, while the corrosion rate will be elevated due to localized galvanic attack. The total degradation (mass loss or depth of damage) is expected to be significantly higher in the multi‐phase structure, though the precise magnitude is uncertain.
generation.baseline: A homogenized single‐phase high‐entropy alloy of the same or closely matched composition (with minimized phase segregation), in which galvanic effects are suppressed.
generation.boundary: Tests performed under controlled conditions: temperature maintained at 450–650 °C; exposure to the same corrosive medium (e.g., acidic or molten salt environment) and identical wear loading conditions; sample size, duration, and testing geometry are standardized.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative increase in degradation rates is uncertain and will depend on the degree of phase contrast and the specific wear/corrosion test parameters. Also, the balance between wear removal and oxide reformation at high temperature may influence the net effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples with identical overall compositions: one set processed to maintain the inherent eutectic (multi‐phase) microstructure and a second set processed via homogenization (e.g., post-casting heat treatment) to achieve a predominantly single-phase structure. Subject both sets to identical simultaneous wear and corrosion tests under elevated temperature (450–650 °C) in the same corrosive environment and with equivalent mechanical wear loads and cycling.
measurements: Total mass loss or depth of degradation over time
Wear track morphology and volume loss (via microscopy and profilometry)
Electrochemical corrosion metrics (e.g., current density, potential mapping)
Surface analysis for evidence of selective phase damage (using SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multi-phase eutectic samples do not show a significantly greater rate of degradation (in terms of both wear and corrosion metrics) relative to the homogenized single-phase baseline under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis—that accelerated degradation is driven by micro-galvanic coupling at phase boundaries—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
